title: Transfer: Find the Minimum of a Rotated Sorted Array
oneLiner: No target this time: find the smallest value of a rotated sorted array in O(log n) by keeping whichever half still holds the drop.
keyTakeaway: The minimum sits just after the one drop. Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]: if nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop is to the right of mid, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left, so hi = mid. Stop when lo == hi.
explanation:
This follows Search a Rotated Sorted Array with the requirement changed: there is no target. Given a sorted array of distinct integers that was rotated an unknown number of times (possibly zero), return its smallest value in O(log n). For [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] the answer is 0. The array has at least one element.

The parent lesson's insight still holds: the array is two sorted runs with a single drop between them, and the minimum is the first value after the drop. So instead of asking "which half could hold the target?", ask "which half holds the drop?".

Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the values drop somewhere between mid and hi, so the drop, and the minimum, are strictly to the right of mid: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise nums[mid] < nums[hi], so mid..hi is one sorted run; the minimum is mid itself or something to its left: hi = mid (not mid - 1, because mid may be the answer). Loop while lo < hi; when they meet, nums[lo] is the minimum.

Why compare with hi and not lo, as the parent did? Because nums[lo] < nums[mid] is true both for [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] cut at 7 (minimum to the right) and for an array that was never rotated, [1, 2, 3, 4] (minimum at lo). One comparison can't tell those apart. nums[mid] versus nums[hi] always can, since the right end is the last value of whichever run it sits in.

The loop shape changes too: while lo < hi with hi = mid, rather than while lo <= hi with mid excluded on both sides. You are not checking for equality with a target; you are narrowing a range that always contains the answer until it has one element.

The visualization runs [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]; the highlighted cells are the range lo..hi.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with the parent lesson. Why is half the range still safe to throw away each step, why is it hi = mid here instead of hi = mid - 1, and what does comparing with nums[hi] tell you that comparing with nums[lo] can't?

visualizationSteps.message: Find the minimum. The range lo = 0, hi = 6 always contains it; shrink it until one cell is left.
mid = 3: nums[mid] = 7 > nums[hi] = 2, so the values drop somewhere after mid. The minimum is right of mid: lo = 4.
mid = 5: nums[mid] = 1 < nums[hi] = 2, so mid..hi is sorted. The minimum is mid or left of it: hi = 5.
mid = 4: nums[mid] = 0 < nums[hi] = 1, so mid..hi is sorted. The minimum is mid or left of it: hi = 4.
lo == hi == 4: one cell left, so nums[4] = 0 is the minimum. 3 comparisons for 7 values.

recognitionSignals: "Sorted, then rotated", and the question is about the rotation itself: the minimum, the maximum, or how many times it was rotated.
An O(log n) requirement on an array that is sorted except for one drop.
gotchas: Setting hi = mid - 1 when nums[mid] < nums[hi] can step past the minimum, because mid itself may be it.
Comparing nums[mid] with nums[lo] can't tell "rotated, minimum on the right" from "not rotated, minimum at lo".
Use while lo < hi, not lo <= hi: with hi = mid, lo <= hi never ends once they meet.
confusableWith: Binary Search: Search a Rotated Sorted Array looks for a target, so it checks which half is sorted and whether the target is inside it. Here there is no target, so each step just keeps the half that contains the drop.

complexity.note: Each comparison of nums[mid] with nums[hi] keeps one half of lo..hi, so about log₂ n steps; only lo, hi and mid are stored.
